## When does a replicated store answer "done"? {#part-replication}

A recap of L12: one leader, two followers, and when the leader confirms a write.

```quizdown
---
shuffle_answers: true
---

## A ticket app keeps seat availability in a store with one leader and two followers. The app sends the leader a write: seat 14C is sold. For each situation, choose the kind of replication that produces it. Each option may be used once, more than once, or not at all.

- Leader answers "done" only after both followers have the change :: Synchronous
  > A confirmed write survives the loss of the leader, because both followers have it. A majority would have answered after the first follower had the change.
- Leader fails right after answering "done", before any follower has the change, and the write is lost :: Asynchronous
  > A confirmed write that only the leader had is lost when a follower without it takes over.
- Leader answers "done" after the faster of its two followers has the change :: Majority (quorum)
  > Two of three replicas have it, so losing any one replica keeps the write. DynamoDB works this way. The leader waited for one follower, which asynchronous replication never does.
- Leader answers "done" right after its own commit, while it sends the change to the followers :: Asynchronous
  > The leader waits for no follower, so writes are fast, and a confirmed write may exist only on the leader.
- Every confirmed write survives the loss of any one replica, and one slow follower does not delay writes :: Majority (quorum)
  > The leader waits for one of its two followers, so every confirmed write is on two of the three replicas, and losing any one still leaves a copy. The leader does not wait for the slower follower, which gets the change a little later. Synchronous replication also keeps the write safe, but there the slow follower delays every write.
- One slow follower makes every write wait :: Synchronous
  > The leader cannot answer until every follower it waits for has the change, so the slowest one sets the pace.
- :: Linearizable
  > Linearizability is about what a read may return after a write has finished. It does not say how many followers must have the change before the leader answers "done".
```


## What may the buyer's read return? {#part-reads}

A recap of L12: a follower that is behind, and the two kinds of DynamoDB read.

```quizdown
---
shuffle_answers: true
---

## A ticket app keeps seat availability in DynamoDB. The seller marks seat 14C "sold" and reads it back with a strongly consistent read: "sold". No other write changes seat 14C. The seller then texts the buyer. A moment later the buyer's app reads seat 14C, the request is served by a follower that is behind, and it gets "available". Which statements are true? Select all that apply.

- [x] Buyer's read is not linearizable
    > The buyer's read started after the seller's read had returned "sold", and no later write changed the seat. A linearizable read would have to return "sold".
- [x] Buyer's app used an eventually consistent read
    > A strongly consistent read goes to the leader. A read served by a follower that is behind was an eventually consistent read.
- [x] Strongly consistent read by the buyer would have returned "sold"
    > In DynamoDB a strongly consistent read goes to the leader, which has the latest write.
- [ ] Strongly consistent read uses the same read units as an eventually consistent one
    > A strongly consistent read uses 1 read unit per 4 KB, and an eventually consistent read uses 0.5.
- [ ] Strongly consistent reads alone stop two buyers from both buying seat 14C
    > Both buyers can read "available" correctly at the same moment, then both write. Preventing that needs a conditional write, which checks and writes in one step.
```


## What reaches each copy? {#part-changes}

Polling, the change stream and the outbox, after a few fast changes and one delete.

```quizdown
---
shuffle_answers: true
---

## Between two polls, within one minute, the trips API moves trip t-0042 from accepted to arrived to started. The trips API is the application that owns the table: with each change it makes, it also writes an outbox row. Then a cleanup job removes the item for trip t-0091, which every copy already holds, from the table. The cleanup job writes to the table itself, without the trips API. For each way of getting changes out, choose what reaches the copy. Not all options will be used.

- Poll the table every 5 minutes on an updated-at column :: Latest status only, without the delete
  > Each poll sees only the state at the moment it asks, so the two changes between two polls reach the copy as one. A deleted item matches no query, so the copy never learns of the delete.
- Read the table's change stream :: Every status change, with the delete
  > The stream is the store's own record of changes. It carries every change in order for each item, including deletes, whoever made them.
- Write an outbox row in the same transaction as each change the trips API makes :: Every status change, without the delete
  > The outbox holds only what the trips API wrote. The cleanup job wrote no outbox row, so the copy never learns of the delete.
- :: Latest status only, with the delete
  > Only the stream sees a deleted item. A poll finds nothing to return, and the outbox holds only what the trips API wrote.
- :: Nothing until tomorrow's export
  > That is what a nightly export gives. Each of these three ways gets changes to the copy within minutes or seconds.
```


## Which way meets each requirement with the slowest refresh? {#part-requirements}

Data latency requirements in EARS, and the ways to keep a copy up to date.

Fresher data is never free. A copy refreshed more often needs more loads, or an always-on stream of changes, and with them more maintenance concerns and costs. So if these constraints matter, for each reader we may choose the slowest refresh that still meets its requirement. We pay only for the freshness the reader needs, and we keep the simplest way that works.

```quizdown
---
shuffle_answers: true
---

## A food-delivery app keeps its orders in DynamoDB and copies them out in the ways listed below. Each of the two 20-minute ways to export finishes a load before the next one starts. The daily load runs from 02:00 to 03:00 and adds the previous day's orders. For each requirement, choose the way with the slowest refresh that still meets it. If two ways refresh equally often, choose the cheaper one. Each option may be used once, more than once, or not at all.

- WHEN the monthly invoice runs on the 1st at 06:00, INVOICING SHALL include every order delivered before the 1st at 00:00 :: Data lake, daily partitions
  > The 02:00 load adds the finished day and finishes by 03:00, so every order delivered before 00:00 is in by 06:00. A fresher way adds nothing the invoice needs.
- WHILE orders are open, KITCHEN SCREEN SHALL show each new order with data latency under 10 s at p99 :: Streaming
  > A load takes minutes, so even an order placed just before one misses 10 s. Only a stream gets each change to the reader within seconds.
- WHILE the restaurant is open, DASHBOARD SHALL show orders with data latency under 1 h at p95 :: Lakehouse, delete files, every 20 min
  > A 20-minute load meets the hour with time to spare, and readers always see one whole snapshot. A daily load can be a day behind. The data lake rewritten every 20 minutes meets the hour too, but exports the whole table on every run. A stream also meets the hour, with more freshness than the dashboard needs.
- WHEN the tax report runs at 06:00 the day after a quarter ends, REPORT SHALL include every order of the quarter :: Data lake, daily partitions
  > The daily load of the quarter's last day finishes by 03:00, so every order is in by 06:00. A fresher way adds nothing the report needs.
- WHILE couriers are on shift, DISPATCH SHALL see each order's status with data latency under 30 s at p95 :: Streaming
  > 30 seconds is far below a 20-minute schedule. Each status change has to reach dispatch as it happens.
- WHEN a manager opens the shift summary, SUMMARY SHALL show sales with data latency under 1 h at p99 :: Lakehouse, delete files, every 20 min
  > A change waits at most 20 minutes for the next load, and that load ends before the next one starts. So we expect every change in the copy within 40 minutes, which is under 1 h even at p99. Daily partitions can be a day behind. The data lake rewritten every 20 minutes also meets the hour, but each run exports the whole table, so the lakehouse is the cheaper of the two.
- :: Data lake, rewritten every 20 min
  > It loads every 20 minutes, as the lakehouse does. But each run exports the whole table and rewrites the day's files, while the lakehouse copies only the changes, so the rewrite is the more expensive of the two. Readers can also see half-replaced files while it runs.
```
